title: How Do Estate Administration Attorneys Support Families? Explained (September 2026)
summary: Estate administration attorneys guide families through items such as probate, creditor claims, and asset distribution. Learn more in September 2026.
body_markdown:
When someone dies, an estate administration attorney handles the legal side of settling their estate. This includes opening probate, managing creditor claims, tax matters, and overseeing asset distribution. Whether full representation is needed depends on the size and complexity of the estate. **** This guide covers key points for families and[executors](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/information-for-executors) to know, including: what an estate administration attorney helps with, how fees are structured, what happens during probate, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Estate administration attorneys handle post-death legal work, including: probate, creditor claims, tax matters, and asset distribution.
- Estates that include real property, contested assets, multi-state accounts, or assets approaching tax thresholds typically work with an estate administration attorney.
- Larger estates can take nine months to several years to settle, depending on complexity and state procedure.
- Elayne handles the administrative layer before attorney review, organizing documents and searching across 100+ financial sources.


## Estate Administration Attorney vs. Estate Planning Attorney: Understanding the Difference


Estate planning attorneys help with tasks such as drafting wills, creating trusts, setting up powers of attorney, and structuring an estate to minimize taxes and smooth the eventual transfer of assets.


Estate administration attorneys, sometimes called probate attorneys, guide executors and personal representatives through the[estate administration process](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-is-estate-administration) . This can include: opening probate, notifying creditors, managing the estate inventory, and distributing assets to beneficiaries.


Some attorneys practice both areas, but the work is distinct. Estate planning happens during life. Estate administration happens after death.

## What Does an Estate Administration Attorney Do?


During estate administration, an attorney's work can span across different areas, such as court proceedings, fiduciary guidance, tax matters, and asset distribution.


There are several core responsibilities an attorney may handle, including:


- Petitioning the probate court and securing Letters Testamentary, which grant the executor legal authority to act on the estate's behalf
- Advising the personal representative on[executor fiduciary duties](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-does-an-executor-of-a-will-actually-do-a-complete-guide-to-executor-duties) , including collecting assets, paying valid debts, and distributing what remains to heirs
- Issuing Notice to Creditors and managing the claims process
- Overseeing tax matters such as preparing the final personal income tax return, the estate income return (Form 1041), and Form 706 where applicable
- Overseeing the inventory and appraisal of estate assets and distributing them to beneficiaries once debts and taxes are resolved


The scope of involvement varies by arrangement and estate. Some attorneys serve in an advisory role, guiding the personal representative through decisions and filings. Others handle procedural work directly, including court filings, creditor communications, and asset transfers.


## What Happens During Probate


Probate opens when the personal representative files a petition with the[probate court](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-is-probate-court) , typically within 30 to 90 days of the decedent's passing. The court validates the will, appoints the executor, and issues[Letters Testamentary](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-are-letters-testamentary) . From there, the estate moves through asset inventory, creditor notification, debt resolution, tax filings, and final distribution to heirs.


When there is no will, the estate passes through intestate administration instead. The court appoints an administrator, and state law determines who inherits.


Probate procedure varies by state and even by county. Court forms, filing requirements, creditor notice windows, and clerk expectations can differ across jurisdictions.

## How an Estate Administration Attorney Helps During Probate


A simple estate with few assets, no real property, and cooperative heirs may not require attorney involvement. However, there are many situations where working with an attorney can be be especially helpful, including when:


- The estate includes real property, business interests, or financial accounts in more than one state
- The will is being contested or beneficiaries disagree about how assets should be distributed
- The estate has substantial debt or creditor claims that may be larger than what the estate can cover
- A trust needs to be administered alongside probate, or instead of it
- There is no will and figuring out who inherits is complicated by multiple factors


After a death, an estate attorney works through a set of legal and administrative steps. The timeline varies based on the size of the estate and the probate rules in the relevant state.


For example, in the first week after a death, the focus is typically on securing assets and gathering[certified death certificates](https://www.usa.gov/death-certificate) . The personal representative notifies the Social Security Administration to stop benefit payments, contacts financial institutions to flag accounts, and may initiate a credit freeze to protect against identity theft.


The attorney files the probate petition and pursues Letters Testamentary. Once the court grants authority, the personal representative can access accounts, transfer titled property, and begin the formal inventory. This stage involves a significant volume of[executor of estate paperwork](https://www.elayne.com/resources/executor-of-estate-paperwork) . The attorney also handles[notice to creditors](https://www.elayne.com/resources/notice-to-creditors-requirements) filings, tracks the creditor claim window, and advises on which debts the estate is required to pay and which claims may be disputed.


Tax filings proceed alongside probate. The attorney works with a CPA to handle the decedent's final Form 1040, a Form 1041 if the estate earns income during administration, and Form 706 if the gross estate meets the federal filing threshold. State income or estate tax returns may also be required based on the decedent's state of residence and where property was held.


Once debts and taxes are resolved, the attorney prepares the final accounting and oversees distribution to beneficiaries. For inherited retirement accounts, the attorney advises on SECURE Act 2.0 rules, including annual required minimum distributions (RMDs).

## FAQ


### What's the difference between an estate planning attorney and an estate administration attorney?


An estate planning attorney works on tasks such as drafting wills, trusts, and powers of attorney. An estate administration attorney (sometimes called a probate attorney) steps in after someone has died to guide executors through tasks such as probate, creditor notifications, tax matters, and asset distribution.


### How does an estate attorney help families after someone dies?


Attorneys support families in many areas, including when it comes to filing a probate petition, working toward Letters Testamentary, overseeing the Notice to Creditors process, and coordinating tax filings. Once debts and taxes are resolved, the attorney prepares the final accounting and oversees distribution to beneficiaries.


### Do I need to work with an estate attorney if the estate is relatively small or straightforward?


Estates with few assets, no real property, and heirs who agree on distribution may be able to go through probate without full legal representation. However, attorney involvement becomes especially helpful when the estate includes real property in more than one state, a contested will, significant creditor claims, a trust that needs to be administered, or potential federal or state estate tax liability. A consultation with a local probate attorney can help families determine what level of help a specific estate requires.


### What is the difference between a personal representative and an executor?


An executor is named in a will to carry out its instructions. A personal representative is the broader legal term for whoever the court appoints to administer an estate, whether or not a will exists. When there is no will, the court appoints an administrator.


### Does an estate always have to go through probate?


No. Assets with named beneficiaries—such as life insurance policies, retirement accounts, and payable-on-death bank accounts—pass directly to those beneficiaries without going through probate. Assets held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship also transfer outside of probate. Only assets titled solely in the decedent's name, with no beneficiary designation, typically need to go through the probate process.


### How long does probate usually take?


Timelines vary widely depending on the state, the size of the estate, and whether any disputes arise. A straightforward estate in a state with a simplified probate process can close in a few months. A larger or more complex estate can take a year or more.


### What happens if someone dies without a will?


When there is no will, the estate is considered intestate. State law determines who inherits, following a fixed order of priority—typically a spouse, then children, then other relatives. The probate court appoints an administrator to carry out the distribution.


### What does an estate attorney charge?


Fee structures vary by attorney and by state. Some states allow attorneys to charge a percentage of the gross estate value, set by statute. Others bill by the hour, or have flat fees.


### What is Letters Testamentary?


Letters Testamentary is a legal document issued by the probate court after it appoints the executor. It gives the executor formal authority to act on behalf of the estate—opening estate bank accounts, accessing financial accounts, transferring titled property, and handling other legal and financial steps. Without it, financial institutions and government agencies will generally not allow access to or changes in accounts held in the decedent's name.
